title: Good Bishop, Bad Bishop
subtitle: Structure decides the piece's value, not the piece itself
summary: A bishop's value isn't fixed — it's set by which squares its own pawns block. Lock a chain onto your bishop's color and it strangles behind its own pawns; keep the chain off that color and the same piece rules the board. This lesson shows the classic French/Caro-Kann 'problem bishop' and two real ways out: trade it for something better, or get it moving before the door closes.

rootAnnotations.title: Same piece, opposite verdicts
rootAnnotations.body: A bishop is 'bad' when its own side's pawns sit on its color and block its diagonals, and 'good' when they don't. It's the exact same piece either way — a bishop doesn't get worse at moving. What changes is the board around it. The French Defense and Caro-Kann lessons both turn on this single fact for the light-squared bishop: French Black plays ...e6 and locks it in before it escapes; Caro-Kann Black plays ...Bf5 and gets it out first, then plays ...e6. Same structure, opposite piece.

rootAnnotations.title: Not a life sentence
rootAnnotations.body: 'Bad bishop' describes a piece's current diagonals, not its permanent fate. A bad bishop can still be traded for something better, rerouted to a different diagonal, or unlocked the moment its own pawn chain moves or trades off. Writing it off early is itself a mistake.

annotations.body: White simply continues developing. Black's light-squared bishop, still on c8, is already the position's defining feature — blocked in front by its own e6-pawn exactly as the French Defense lesson describes.

annotations.title: Getting out, one tempo late
annotations.body: The ideal fix — developing the bishop before ...e6 is even played, as the Caro-Kann lesson teaches — is no longer available; the pawn chain is already locked. But 'bad' isn't 'stuck': Black spends a tempo opening a second diagonal for the bishop through b7, since the direct route through d7–e6 is walled off by Black's own pawn.
White's own light-squared bishop sits on d3 — good, active, aimed at the kingside. What does Black's bishop want with it?

annotations.title: Remedy one: trade it for the good one
annotations.body: The bishop reaches a6 and stares straight down the long diagonal at White's well-placed bishop on d3. If the trade goes through, Black hands over the piece that had almost nothing to do all game for the piece that had everything to do — a clear upgrade even though the material count reads 'one bishop for one bishop.'
White could grab the trade immediately with Bxa6, but declines for now and continues developing instead — voluntarily avoiding the swap is itself an admission of which bishop is worth more.

annotations.title: Cashing in
annotations.body: Black completes the trade. Two tempi — ...b6 and ...Ba6 — bought the exchange of the bad bishop for the good one, a fair price for permanently fixing the position's worst piece.

annotations.title: What you should have noticed
annotations.body: Three lessons: a bishop's color relative to its own locked pawns, not its raw mobility on an empty board, decides good or bad — the same French/Caro-Kann structure produces opposite verdicts depending only on move order; trading a bad piece for a good enemy piece is a real remedy even when the material count looks neutral, since points on the scoresheet aren't the same as usefulness on the board; and the fix, whether prevention (Caro-Kann) or a late escape (here), is almost always available in some form — 'bad bishop' describes a moment, not a verdict.
